text: After thirty years of commuting by rail, Mr Pereira did not read the departures board the way the young couple beside him did. He read the lateness of the previous service, the cancelled stop two lines down and the platform that had changed twice since morning, and then he walked down to where the first carriage always stopped. The couple stayed put and lost their seats.

Bed six coughed twice, dry and short, and Bolanle's hand stopped on the drip bag. It was the cough of her old landlady's dog, Biscuit, in a hallway in Peckham, and she could see its green lead hanging on the radiator hook. She had not thought of that dog since she moved out. She checked the man's chart, then his oxygen, and smoothed the blanket over his feet.

A thin mist lay over the lower pasture at first light, and the grass under it was heavy with water. Sheep stood in a loose group near the gate with beads of wet along their backs. In the yard the tractor ticked as its engine cooled, a drop of diesel swelling under the tank cap. Along the stone wall a trickle of rainwater found a gap, crossed the lane and pooled in a rut.

At every lunch break Bianca, in her second year as a developer, drifted toward the corner where the senior designer sketched layouts in coloured pens, and she lingered behind his chair for as long as she dared. She kept away from the server room, whose cold air and roaring fans made her shoulders hunch. The director's ten-minute talk about a company restructure went past her, but one curt line about her code in a stranger's email kept her awake until two.

Teodor had cooked on cargo ships for thirty years, and he tasted the new soup with his eyes shut. The carrot was sweet enough, he told the young cook, but the stock was thin, the cream had gone in too early, and the onion had not been given long enough to turn soft. She copied each piece onto the back of her hand with a marker and went back to the stove to start the soup over.

The band had met on Tuesdays and Thursdays at seven for three years, and by now Lena's hands were on her fiddle before she had finished taking off her coat. At the words 'from the top' her bow arm lifted and her left foot found the floor. At her sister's wedding the room fell quiet for the toasts, and she caught her fingers tuning against the stem of her glass.

Under the van, with a spanner on a seized bolt, Wendell heard the radiator fan clatter and was suddenly eight years old, pegging a torn seven of clubs to the spokes of his brother's red bike. He had not thought of that bike in forty years. He could see the gravel lane behind their father's shed and feel the scrape on his knee. The bolt gave with a crack, and he slid out smiling at the ceiling.

setting: a family home on a weekend
text: Everything Imelda knew about money she had learned from her mother, who counted coins into jam jars on Friday nights, so when her husband brought up a new car on a four-year loan she did not hear a car. She heard the jars. She asked for the interest figure and the monthly figure, then wrote three columns on the back of an envelope.

Between customers, Joseph kept sliding back to one crate of old jazz sleeves on his folding table, thumbing the corners and lifting them to his nose. He turned his chair away from the stall opposite, where a man fried onions in a drum of black fat, and breathed through his mouth. A child dropped a whole box of singles on the pavement beside him, and Joseph hardly glanced down.

Every Thursday for two years Hamza had been sent out to run the mile on the field behind the school, and by spring his hands bent to his laces before anyone spoke. They did it mid-sentence while he argued about football. On the week of the exams, when the mile was cancelled, he found himself on the bench outside the maths room with one trainer already off.

The attendant's tea came in a glass with a metal holder, and the holder took Galina straight back to an exam hall in Omsk, where she had failed a physics paper and wept afterward in the courtyard. She sipped slowly as the sidings of Novosibirsk slid by. The number on her desk had been forty-one, and a pale patch of sunlight had lain across the floor.

Ingrid, who had inherited the farm at twenty-six, was drawn every dawn to the henhouse, where warm eggs lay in the straw and the birds muttered in the half dark. She skirted the slurry pit with her sleeve against her face and left the pig shed to her brother whenever she could. When the vet rang to say the bull's test had come back bad, she said fine, fine, and was still humming when she put the phone down.

The walk-in cooler hummed through the empty hours before dawn. Every few minutes the compressor shuddered, the fan blades spun faster, and a thin line of frost thickened along the pipe above the door. Crates of milk stacked against the back wall lost the last of their warmth. At the far end, a drop fell from the edge of a shelf into a steel tray about once every forty seconds.

Sister Fatima had trained when patients lay flat for ten days after surgery, and she still felt uneasy watching the young physio stand a man up on his second morning. She watched his colour, his lips, the way his knuckles whitened on the frame. She had seen two decades of recoveries go badly and three go wonderfully, and she slid a chair in behind him without being asked.

Anneliese came in two beats late on the chorus. The drummer's snare had rattled against the window glass in the second verse, and she had been in a hailstorm over a Swiss campsite twenty summers ago, tent poles shaking, a mug of cold tea in her hand. The bassist raised one eyebrow and kept his line.

The build server at Parkway Software sounded a loud chime whenever a test run failed, and in eighteen months it had chimed hundreds of times. At the sound, Ayesha's right hand moved to her mouse, her eyes went to the second monitor, and she opened the log before she finished her sentence. A visiting client flinched at the chime and asked what it was, and Ayesha, already scrolling, asked him what he meant.

setting: a family home on a weekend
text: Sunday afternoon kept pulling Delroy toward the garage, where his half-built canoe lay on trestles, and three times before lunch he found himself standing over it with a plane in his hand. The vacuum cleaner in the hall made his skin crawl, so he went out to the garden whenever his wife switched it on. His daughter slammed her bedroom door hard enough to knock a photograph off the wall, and he turned a page of the newspaper.

The Corsa would start, run for ten minutes and die. Gordon laid it out for the apprentice in pieces: fuel was reaching the rail, the spark was strong, the crank sensor read fine when cold, and trouble only came once the engine bay was fully hot. That left one part that failed only in the heat and never showed on the code reader. He tapped the wiring loop behind the block with the handle of a screwdriver.

By six in the morning the vans had backed up along the kerb, and crates of onions, cabbages and shrink-wrapped trays rolled down ramps onto trestle tables. Canvas roofs snapped taut on their poles. A pallet jack squealed under a stack of tomato boxes, tipped them against a wall and was dragged away. Water from a hose ran along the gutter, carrying leaves and a paper cup toward the drain.

In the second row a boy clicked his pen twice, fast, and Priya, halfway through handing back chemistry tests, was suddenly on a cold balcony in Leicester. Her father had clicked his lighter exactly that way before he gave up smoking, and she could smell the wool of his coat. She finished returning the papers. The boy never found out where she had been.

Alasdair had farmed through three droughts, and when the forecast promised a wet week he did not feel relief. He looked at the slope of the lower field, remembered the autumn the topsoil washed into the ditch, and told his son to move the ewes uphill before dark. His son, who was twenty, saw only rain and said it would be good for the grass.

Ten-year-old Tobias spent most of the twelve-hour journey pressed against the window, following the freight yards and cranes and every bridge that flashed past. He turned his shoulder to the man across the aisle who was peeling boiled eggs, and pulled his jacket over his nose each time a shell cracked. When the train jolted to a halt in open country for forty minutes, he barely lifted his head.

For six years Cheng had washed his hands at the same sink at the start of every shift, wrists first, then palms, thumbs and between the fingers. On holiday in Portugal he found himself doing it at a cafe washbasin while his wife waited outside. The waiter watched him walk back to the table still counting to twenty under his breath.

A smell of scorched sugar drifted over from the pastry corner, and Dariusz, reducing a veal stock, was nine years old again, standing on a chair in his grandmother's flat in Lodz while she browned sugar in a dented pan for the Christmas cake. He could see the blue oilcloth and hear the radio on the sill. The stock caught on the bottom of the pot, and he lifted it off the heat a moment too late.

Kwame had played in wedding bands since he was fifteen, and when the new singer handed round a song that kept changing its count, he did not look at the notes first. He looked at her foot and at the way her shoulders moved at the barline, and he recalled forty Saturday nights when the dancers had got lost at exactly this kind of switch. In pencil he marked a bar of rest on his chart.

setting: a family home on a weekend
text: For eleven years the Okafors had eaten Sunday lunch at one, and the smell of onions frying at half past twelve had become the signal that sent everyone into the kitchen. The boys no longer needed calling. The older one put down his game and the younger one left his drawing, and both stood by the table with forks in hand on the Sunday the oven had broken and nothing was cooking.

The old Triumph on the ramp pulled at Imani, seventeen and new to the garage: she ran her thumb along the cracked leather of the seat and bent close to smell the oil. She kept out of the back corner where diesel fumes hung low, and she wrinkled her nose every time the paint-stripper tin was opened. When her boss read out an estimate of four thousand pounds, she nodded without hearing it and kept her eyes on the dashboard dials.

Someone at stand-up called it the old billing job, and Rafael found himself thinking, with no link he could trace, of the lost-property cupboard at his school in Valparaiso: a cardboard box of single gloves, the left ones never claimed. He wondered whether the billing job was the same, a drawer of orphaned pieces. He turned back to his laptop and started searching the tracker for tasks nobody had picked up.

Ms Kowalczyk had worked as a supply teacher for twenty-two years, and when the new head announced a silent-corridor rule she thought of the five schools where she had seen one begin and the four where it was dropped by Easter. She nodded through the staff meeting. The younger teachers looked at the printed plan with real hope, while she looked at the map and counted the stairwells where nobody could see.

Two stalls along, a stranger's phone began to play a tinny waltz. Lucia, weighing apricots, was at her wedding in a village hall near Bari, with white tablecloths and a cousin dancing in odd socks. Two extra apricots went into the bag without her noticing. The customer thanked her, puzzled, and she smiled at the scales.

The night train ran north through flat country, its wheels beating over the joints in the rail. Condensation gathered along the window frames and slid down in crooked lines. When the carriage swayed, a bag of oranges slipped off the luggage rack, rolled to the end of the aisle and stopped against the door. Outside, a single signal lamp changed from green to red and dropped behind into the dark.

The char on the grill steaks pulled at Marisol, nineteen and three weeks into her first kitchen job, and she found reasons to pass the station all shift. She walked the long way round the fish counter, holding her breath whenever the fishmonger's box was opened and the sea bass stared up with flat grey eyes. The head chef's long talk about portion costs went past her, and ten minutes later she could not have repeated a word.

Three days after his hip operation, seventy-one-year-old Gareth kept turning toward the window where the sun lay across the bed, and he asked twice whether the blind could stay up. He pushed the tray of grey mince and boiled cabbage away with two fingers. The surgeon talked for several minutes about the next steps, and the words ran through him. Then a cleaner in the corridor began to hum a hymn from his childhood, and he stopped breathing for a moment.

Kenji had a staple gun in one hand and a sagging fence wire in the other when the sour smell of silage came across the field. It brought Mrs Ohara, who had kept him behind to sweep her classroom for drawing a cow on the board. He had not thought of her in decades. He remembered the broom handle, taller than he was, and the chalk dust in his nose.

The old upright piano drew Tomas across the room, and he kept sliding his stool toward it, where the low notes shook the floor through his shoes. He dragged his case to the far wall, away from the smell of the synthesiser's overheated power brick. The singer burst into tears over a missed cue and he did not look up, yet a cymbal tipping off its stand made him jump so hard his pick flew across the room.

Hiroshi had cleaned up after a dozen failed launches in fifteen years, so when the manager called the new release simple, his first thought was of the three that had been called simple before. On the whiteboard he broke the plan into pieces: the database move, the old mobile app, the Friday timing, the single colleague who understood the payment code. He circled the last one twice.

Rain ran off the corrugated roof in a steady sheet and spilled over a blocked gutter at the corner. In the back room the compressor kicked on, filled its tank and clicked off. A bay door rattled in its frame each time the wind pushed the puddle across the forecourt. Under the lift, oil dripped from a worn gasket onto a flattened cardboard box, spreading a dark ring about the size of a saucer.

setting: a family home on a weekend
text: Ruth stood with the butter knife in her hand until the toast went cold. The back gate had squeaked, long and low, and it had brought her late husband's bicycle with it, the way he leaned it on the fence and whistled the same four notes. Her granddaughter, who was five, asked if the gate was broken, and Ruth said it was only talking.

Nasreen had run a spice stall for forty years, and when the council's new rent letter arrived she did not read it as a paragraph. She read it as three separate pieces: a pitch fee up by a fifth, a clause about insurance, and a Saturday closing time that would cut off the crowd leaving the church. She circled each one in red and slid the sheet under the cumin tin.

All the way to the gym Owen dragged his feet, but at the art room, with its propped-open door and its smell of wet clay, his stride doubled. He took the long way round the music corridor, where a trombone was being tortured, and pressed a sleeve to one ear. Mr Adeyemi read the detention list at assembly, Owen's name among them, and Owen went on drawing a horse on the back of his hand.
